children: KFC India’s ChatGPT presence and McDonald’s digital menu-board advertising are prompting marketers to rethink how brands influence discovery, consideration and conversion

When a consumer asks an AI assistant where to eat tonight, or glances at a digital menu board while queuing for lunch, a brand has a few seconds to influence what happens next. Marketers are increasingly treating those moments as media inventory.

KFC India has begun advertising on ChatGPT, placing the brand inside an AI-led discovery journey. In the US, McDonald’s is testing third-party advertising on digital menu boards at 450 company-owned restaurants through its McDonald’s Media Network, which the company sees as a potential $1 billion business opportunity.
What Is Pushing Brands In
For Anil Dua, COO, Usha International, the trigger is consumer behaviour.

“The biggest driver is the rapid shift in consumer behaviour and discovery journeys, with consumers increasingly using AI and Generative AI platforms to discover, evaluate and make decisions. This is pushing brands and organisations to invest in AI platforms and initiatives to stay ahead of a disruption that has already arrived.”

“Organisations are mindful of the threat of ‘AI Darwinism’, where consumer behaviour changes faster than the ability of organisations to transform. Investments are therefore being made across areas such as creative renaissance, personalised content, agentic workflows and generative engine visibility. The real opportunity is to move from simply being seen to being considered, by participating in the consumer journey in useful, contextual and credible ways.”
Jyoti Kumar Bansal, chief, brand and communications at Tata Power, describes the same shift from the consumer’s side.

“A business is built when a brand is chosen. And as the consumer changes how and where she discovers, evaluates and buys a brand, the battlefield and the opportunity are changing too. Attention remains the currency, but presence at the moment of decision is the gold.”

“The quiet change is the boundaries between awareness, consideration and conversion are beginning to collapse. The funnel is becoming shorter, less linear and, increasingly, self-feeding. AI platforms, commerce platforms and experiences are all enabling discovery, consideration and choice.”

“The fundamentals of brand, however, remain unchanged. I choose brands that are relevant to my life, useful to me and make me feel good about myself. What is changing is how brands find me, build trust and, increasingly, how they show up through the AI agent that helps me make choices.”
Spend And Returns: Still A Test-and-learn Game

Neither KFC India nor McDonald’s has publicly detailed what these placements cost or what they return, and McDonald’s $1 billion figure is a statement of potential rather than reported revenue. Dua says the wider market is in a similar position.

“Most brands are still experimenting, so there is no universal benchmark for investment yet. There are, however, significant high-profile brand partnerships with tech/AI companies such as OpenAI, Google Gemini and Perplexity, which are also being used to position organisations as first movers.”

“The investment numbers are mostly not public, but many brands are allocating spends across AI initiatives and even hiring Chief AI Officer roles to drive adoption. At this stage, these investments are largely being approached as test-and-learn initiatives, with budgets linked to the scale and strategic importance of the consumer journey.”
On returns, he cautions against reading too much into early results.

“Most brands experimenting with AI are currently measuring ROI through pilots. However, short-term pilots can primarily provide direction for the next move; meaningful impact will come when these initiatives are deployed at scale, where the value of AI lies in its ability to ‘scale to infinity’.”
Rethinking Measurement
If the funnel is collapsing, the scorecard has to change with it.

“Measurement also needs to evolve. Traditional metrics such as clicks, impressions, CTR and CPM may become less relevant in AI-led environments. Marketers will increasingly need to look at quality of engagement, consideration, qualified actions, assisted conversions, incremental sales and ultimately cost per business outcome. Consumer engagement may also need to be viewed across the life continuum of the brand rather than at a single transaction or juncture.”
Which box does it belong in?
The harder question is classification: is advertising inside an AI platform experiential, digital, retail media, or something else? Dua says no single bucket fits.

“These formats do not fit neatly into a single existing bucket. They have elements of digital marketing, commerce media, experiential marketing and CRM, while also being used to scale creative and personalised content, improve targeting and retargeting, enable agentic AI workflows and generate predictive consumer insights.”

“The common thread is that brands are trying to move closer to the consumer’s moment of intent. Commerce media connects brands with consumers closer to purchase, while AI platforms can potentially take this one step earlier - influencing discovery, recommendation and consideration. As AI becomes more embedded across marketing, departments are also being redefined and roles are evolving. While creation is becoming increasingly intrinsic, uniqueness and relevance will become key to success.”
Shubhranshu Singh, marketing strategist, board member, columnist and founder of Prakamya, also advises against forcing an answer.
“On classification, I would resist forcing these formats into old boxes. McDonald’s menu boards are commerce media in their purest form, a business monetising its own footfall and first-party data.”

“Advertising inside AI platforms is something newer and more boosting of returns as it combines the intent of search, the persuasion of advertising and the trust of a recommendation but that last element carries real risk. If consumers begin to feel an assistant’s answer has been bought, the platform loses credibility, and so does the brand inside it.”
“My guess would be that we are watching the emergence of what I would call ‘decision media’, formats that place a brand at the exact moment a choice is made.”

Dua sees the same blurring of boundaries. “We are seeing a convergence of touchpoints, where the lines between digital, retail, commerce and experiential media are increasingly blurring. As AI platforms deliver micro-personalised results, we could see the emergence of a new layer of marketing that understands consumer needs without being restricted by traditional media boundaries.”

“The fundamental principles of marketing remain unchanged - understanding consumers, creating relevance, building preference and driving conversion. What is changing is where and how these interactions happen. The next generation of marketing will increasingly be about being present wherever the consumer is making a decision - whether that is a search engine, social platform, marketplace, retail environment, brand app or an AI assistant.”
“The key shift is therefore from buying attention to influencing intent, with predictive AI potentially going even further by understanding future consumer needs and the consumer’s next best action.”
Bansal sees the stakes reaching beyond the marketing department.
“The real CEO conversation is no longer about shifting marketing dollars among channels. It is about the right bets that influence the moment of choice today and in the evolving future.”

“It means looking at the investment portfolio differently, where technology, data, brand, product, pricing, promotion, distribution and customer experience converge to create business value. Because the investment creating the choice sits across the CMO, sales, product, technology, trade and operations, and then working together will unlock the full business potential and stakeholder value.”
“The future of brand building is not just winning the attention economy. It’s about winning the Decision economy.”
Singh’s advice is more specific.
“The winners will be brands that earn their place in those moments through relevance and usefulness, treating paid presence as an accelerant rather than a substitute.”
